newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan could face pressure on economy but won't bow.
newsitem.headline: Japan could face pressure on economy but won't bow.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's government could face pressure at home and abroad to keep Japan's economy from stalling if more gloomy data emerges, but few foresee any real change in Tokyo's tight fiscal stance.

"Under the current fiscal and structural reform initiative, to withdraw from that line would be an almost suicidal act for the cabinet," said Takeshi Kiuchi, chief economist at LTCB Research Institute.

Tokyo share prices plummeted on Monday, slicing nearly four percent from the key 225-share Nikkei average. The Nikkei finished the day down 780.28 points at 18,824.18 after racking up its biggest one-day point loss so far in 1997.
Bargain-hunting helped the Nikkei rebound modestly to 19,099.11 on Tuesday, but fears remained that the gains were fragile.

Analysts pointed to a plethora of reasons for Monday's steep drop, including Wall Street's sharp fall on Friday, the yen's rise against the dollar, worries over a racketeer payoff scandal in the financial sector and the absence of giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd from stock trade until Wednesday as part of its punishment for its role in the scandal.
But chief among the culprits, economists said, was a growing belief among investors that the government's guardedly optimistic view of the economy is far too rosy.

"The Finance Ministry had convinced people you can put up taxes and cut spending without an impact on demand," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Barings. "Unfortunately, the data is showing that the economy is in terrible condition."

The Economic Planning Agency said in its monthly report last week that the economy was recovering gradually despite a temporary slowdown caused by a sales tax increase in April. But an agency official admitted that the sales tax rise was having an unexpectedly prolonged impact on consumption.
The tax rise, along with an end to special income tax rebates and cuts in public works spending, is part of Hashimoto's efforts to trim Japan's huge budget deficit.

Market pundits have now grown less inclined to put their faith in the government's soothing words. "They had believed the government view that the tax hike effect would be temporary... Now people are surprised, and when they are surprised they run for the door," said Salomon Brothers Asia chief economist Robert Feldman.

Economists said lacklustre data was likely to keep coming for another quarter or two, with some predicting the economy might even slip back into recession. "There is no impetus for recovery...and the possibility of a recession is quite large," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute.

Others take a cheerier view. "Yes, there is a mini down cycle in place sparked by the tax increase...but this is nothing unexpected and it seems a bit irrational to assume Japan is falling back into a deflationary pit," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.

Gloomy data is sure to spark calls for government action, including from U.S. officials who have consistently urged Japan to ensure its recovery is led by domestic demand and not to let its current account surplus balloon past 2.5 percent of gross domestic product.
"Autumn will be the critical season," Kiuchi said.

Even if the worst-case scenario plays out, however, interest rates are already at rock bottom and economists rule out the old-style public pump-priming steps so often employed in the past, although some said the government might fine-tune its tight fiscal stance to ease the pain.

"In the past five years, every time the economy slumped the government stepped in with a spending package, tax cuts or interest rate reductions or all three. This time, the chances are they will do absolutely nothing," Jerram said.

That means the Tokyo stock market is unlikely to see a dramatic upswing anytime soon. "If some positive economic numbers emerge these would be translated into an upswing in stocks, but not a dramatic one," LTCB's Kiuchi said. "When we look at the bumpy road ahead, the stock market lacks the steam to move forward."
